name: Fejér kernel
short: The nonnegative kernel for averaged Fourier sums.
body: Averaging the first N+1 Dirichlet kernels gives a nonnegative approximation kernel with good convergence properties for continuous periodic functions.
example: For N=1, F₁(θ)=1+cosθ. Its integral with normalized circle measure is 1.
note: Cesàro averaging changes the kernel, rather than simply adding more Fourier modes.

sources.title: Fejér's Theorem and Convergence of Fourier Series

name: Generating-function kernel
short: The coefficient canceled in the kernel method.
body: In functional equations for generating functions, a kernel is a coefficient multiplying the unknown function. The kernel method selects a suitable root that cancels this coefficient and exposes a relation among remaining terms.
example: For a walk step polynomial P(u)=u+u⁻¹, a common kernel is 1−zP(u). One chooses a formal root with the required behavior near z=0.
note: A root cannot be chosen arbitrarily: formal-series and analyticity conditions matter. This kernel method is not machine-learning kernel fitting.

sources.title: Basic analytic combinatorics of directed lattice paths

name: Green kernel / Green's function
short: The response to a point source, with boundary conditions.
body: A Green kernel represents an inverse or solution operator for a differential equation. Integrating the point-source responses builds the response to a distributed source.
example: For −u″=f on (0,1) with u(0)=u(1)=0, G(x,y)=min(x,y)−xy; then u(x)=∫₀¹G(x,y)f(y)dy.
note: The operator, domain and boundary conditions are part of the definition. A Green kernel and an operator's nullspace are different.

name: Hilbert-transform kernel
body: The Hilbert transform uses an odd singular kernel to construct a quadrature counterpart of a real signal. Its convolution is interpreted in the principal-value sense.
example: In a standard convention, H(cosωx)=sinωx for ω>0. This is useful in analytic-signal representations.
note: Normalization and sign conventions vary. This is not the reproducing kernel of an arbitrary Hilbert space.

sources.title: A Short Tour of Harmonic Analysis

name: Interpolation / reconstruction kernel
short: A function used to reconstruct values between samples.
body: A reconstruction kernel builds a continuous approximation from discrete samples. The kernel shape controls sharpness, smoothness and ringing.
example: A triangular kernel gives linear interpolation in one dimension. Ideal bandlimited reconstruction uses sinc(x)=sin(πx)/(πx).
note: Exact sinc reconstruction requires the sampling theorem's assumptions. Bicubic and Lanczos filters are practical alternatives with different tradeoffs.

name: Kernel polynomial method
short: A damping kernel for truncated polynomial expansions.
body: Kernel polynomial methods damp coefficients of truncated Chebyshev expansions to reduce oscillations and obtain useful spectral approximations.
example: Jackson damping suppresses ringing in approximate densities of states. Dirichlet and Lorentz kernels give other damping choices.
note: The displayed series omits application-specific prefactors and normalization. The kernel concerns the expansion, not GPU execution.

name: Kernel-regression weights
short: Weights for fitting or averaging nearby observations.
body: In Nadaraya–Watson regression, a kernel assigns locality weights and their normalized sum gives a predicted mean. Local polynomial regression uses related weights in a local fit.
example: If two response values 10 and 20 receive weights 3 and 1, the local constant prediction is 12.5.
note: This local smoother differs from kernel ridge regression in an RKHS, although both may use Gaussian functions.

name: Memory / friction kernel
short: Weights on the system's past behavior.
body: A memory kernel specifies how past states or velocities influence present evolution. Generalized Langevin equations use such kernels to describe non-instantaneous friction.
example: With Γ(t)=γe⁻ᵗ/τ, recent velocities receive greater weight than distant ones.
note: This is a temporal response function, not a block of computer memory or a GPU routine.

sources.title: Microscopic theory of Brownian motion: Mori friction kernel

name: Mollifier / approximate-identity kernel
short: A scaled kernel that smooths while approaching the identity.
body: A standard mollifier is a smooth, nonnegative, unit-integral bump. Shrinking its scale gives a family whose convolution approximates the original function. Approximate identities form a broader class.
example: Convolving a step with a small smooth bump replaces the jump with a narrow smooth transition.
note: Not every smoothing filter is an approximate identity, and not every approximate identity is a compactly supported smooth mollifier.

name: Poisson kernel
short: Weights that extend boundary values harmonically.
body: A Poisson kernel solves a harmonic boundary-value problem by weighting boundary data. Its form depends on the domain.
example: In the unit disk, integrate Pᵣ against boundary values using dθ/(2π). At r=0, every boundary angle has equal weight.
note: This Poisson kernel is unrelated to Poisson-distributed counts except through broader probabilistic connections.

sources.title: The Poisson kernel on the unit disc

name: Radiation point kernel
short: The detector response to a point radiation source.
body: Point-kernel methods integrate point-source responses over a distributed radiation source. A basic uncollided photon-flux term combines geometric spreading and attenuation; buildup models can approximate scattered contributions.
example: In a homogeneous absorber, the uncollided response falls with inverse-square distance and exponential attenuation.
note: Real shielding calculations require energy, material, geometry and scattering considerations. This formula is an illustrative idealization, not a shield-design prescription.

sources.title: Point-Kernel Code Development for Gamma-Ray Shielding Applications

name: Sensitivity / Fréchet kernel
short: How a model perturbation changes an observation.
body: Linearizing a forward model produces a sensitivity kernel: a spatial weighting of parameter perturbations that predicts a small data change.
example: A seismic travel-time kernel indicates which regions of Earth's structure influence a measurement. Finite-frequency sensitivity can occupy a volume rather than a single ray.
note: It represents a derivative of the forward model, not necessarily the resolution of a retrieved model.

name: Singular / Calderón–Zygmund kernel
short: An operator kernel singular along the diagonal.
body: Singular integral kernels can blow up as x approaches y. Cancellation, principal values and suitable boundedness and regularity conditions make the corresponding operators meaningful.
example: The Hilbert-transform kernel is the one-dimensional prototype. Riesz transforms provide higher-dimensional examples.
note: An arbitrary divergent integral is not automatically a valid singular integral operator.

sources.title: Singular kernels and Calderón–Zygmund operators
sources.publisher: Terence Tao; hosted at Johns Hopkins

name: SPH smoothing kernel
short: A spatial weighting function for particle-based fields.
body: Smoothed particle hydrodynamics approximates continuum fields through a smoothing kernel and particle sums. Smoothing length and kernel shape determine which neighbors contribute and how strongly.
example: A compactly supported spline kernel lets a particle gather information from a finite neighborhood rather than from the entire simulation.
note: The smoothing kernel is a mathematical function. A GPU kernel can execute the particle sum; these are different layers.

name: Stein kernel: integration by parts
short: A function or matrix realizing a Stein identity.
body: For a one-dimensional variable X with mean μ, a Stein kernel τ satisfies an integration-by-parts identity for suitable test functions.
example: For X∼N(μ,σ²), the constant τ(x)=σ² is a Stein kernel. For a uniform variable on [−1,1], τ(x)=(1−x²)/2.
note: This τ is a function of one input. The pairwise Stein kernel used in a kernel Stein discrepancy is another construction.

name: Transform kernel
short: The function against which a transform integrates.
body: Integral transforms change a function's representation by integrating it against a prescribed function of the input and output coordinates.
example: The Fourier kernel is e⁻²πⁱˣξ in this convention; the one-sided Laplace kernel is e⁻ˢᵗ on t≥0.
note: A transform kernel may oscillate, be complex-valued, and have no probability or similarity interpretation. Fourier normalization conventions vary.

sources.title: The Fourier Transform and Laplace Transform

name: Volterra-series kernel
body: A Volterra expansion expresses a nonlinear system through kernels of one, two or more time lags, multiplying corresponding input values before integration.
example: A quadratic response requires a two-lag kernel h₂, whereas an LTI system uses a one-lag impulse response h₁.
note: Volterra can also describe a linear integral operator with a variable integration limit. That usage is an integral-kernel subtype.

sources.title: Nonlinear System Analysis Based on the Volterra Series
sources.publisher: M. Weiss / University of South Wales
